title: Validation of methods for sequencing isolates from patients, drinking water, and wastewater to determine their epidemiological significance and regulation based on this information
summary:
Background
In hospitals, microorganisms can colonize the drinking water and wastewater systems and thereby pose an additional infection risk, especially for vulnerable patient groups. So far, it is insufficiently understood to what extent such water‑associated pathogens are actually linked to hospital‑acquired infections in patients.
​
Research question
The project aims to clarify whether, and to what extent, pathogens detected in the drinking water and wastewater of University Medicine Essen are also found in clinical samples from patients and thus contribute to infections. In addition, it asks which pipe sections or building areas represent particularly relevant contamination and transmission routes from a hygiene perspective.
​
Methods
Over the course of one year, water samples will be taken at defined locations in the drinking water and wastewater system using automatic samplers and examined microbiologically. In parallel, pathogens from already existing diagnostic samples from patients (for example blood cultures, wound swabs, stool samples) will be collected, frozen and then compared with the water isolates using modern genetic methods, without any additional procedures or appointments for the patients.

interventions.name:
The study includes all patients < 18 years of age whose microbiological samples contain reference pathogens.
In this context, reference pathogens are defined as all isolates of:
•    Aeromonas
•    intestinal pathogenic Escherichia coli (EHEC, ETEC, EIEC, EPEC, etc.)
•    non-tuberculous mycobac

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
The study includes all patients < 18 years of age from whom microbiological samples containing the above-mentioned reference pathogens were obtained.

In addition, trauma surgery patients < 18 years of age from whom microbiological samples were obtained from surgical wounds on the lower leg, ankle, and foot or intraoperatively from these body sites and who tested positive for Gram-negative rods and enterococci are included.
